title: Data integrity
description: Is the data we are betting on sound? The unbackfillable capture edge, the reconciler, the continuity sweep, the canonical writers, the admission gate, and the telemetry path that carries all of it. Every panel that serves an alert plots that alert's own expression and carries its own threshold line, so what you see here is the number the page was computed from. Restart markers come from the process-start family; the edge machine publishes none, and nothing on this board plots an edge family either. The default window is seven days because the widest alert on this board looks back 26 hours.

panels.title: Book desync — live and stuck (15m)
panels.description: Which pair's book is checksum-desynced right now, and whether it is in the shape that pages. The live series sits at 1 while a pair's book is desynced; the 15-minute minimum is the series the alert reads, because a desync that healed inside the window carries a zero and reads 0 — recovery is a single fire-and-forget resubscribe fired only on the transition, so a pair whose one attempt did not take stays stuck and nothing retries it. That series pages above 0.5 after `for: 5m`, so roughly twenty minutes in total: a 15-minute window plus the hold. Scoped by the capture-machine and pair pickers.

panels.title: Seconds since last book message (per pair)
panels.description: Per-pair proof of life: which stream has gone quiet and for how long, while it is still a live condition rather than a ledger entry booked hours later. Two page lines for two different faults. The per-machine minimum across every pair crossing 120 seconds means the WHOLE feed is silent — one thin leg being quiet is normal at any hour, every pair at once is not, and nothing in the capture path produces it, which is why that bar can be tight. What does produce it is the venue on a published calendar — both firings so far fell inside an announced Kraken maintenance window — so read that calendar first. It fires with **no hold at all** (`for: 0s`): the gauge is scraped once a minute, so a pending period would spend the entire notice budget rather than buy confidence. A single per-pair series crossing 300 seconds — with no hold either — is the one-stuck-stream shape nothing else catches: the dead-man still pings, the desync rule sees no checksum failure, and the minimum reads off a healthy pair. Every gauge reads 0 at process start, so a restart cannot false-fire either line. The per-pair series follows both pickers; the minimum follows only the machine picker, exactly as its alert evaluates it.

panels.title: Recovery ladder — 24h increase
panels.description: Is the desync recovery path being exercised more than it should be, and does it work? Two page lines, both held for `for: 30m`. Resubscribes over 24 hours above 1.5 mean the rate is re-elevating or a pair is flapping. Rejected frames and missing unsubscribe acks are SUMMED before the same 1.5 line, because that is how the alert evaluates them — one of each is two and pages, while two separate per-counter series would both read green. 1.5 rather than 1 because a single increment extrapolates to about 1.0007 and would page on one genuine self-healed event. Reconnects are context only: no alert watches them. Neither resubscribe counter carries a pair label, so this says THAT the rate rose, not which pair — the desync panel above names the pair. Scoped by the capture-machine picker.

panels.title: Book silence — gap seconds per pair (24h increase)
panels.description: Which pair contributed how much book silence in the last day — the capture-side origin of every healable and residual second booked downstream. The 30-second line is the capture daemon's own derived silence bar, roughly 2.4 times the thinnest leg's worst natural spacing, and it deliberately equals the reconciler's minimum-gap setting. It is **not** an alerting bar: no rule watches this counter per pair, and the reconciler's own 600-second figure is computed on a different metric entirely — an aggregate divided by the live pair count — so it does not belong on this panel. Scoped by the capture-machine and pair pickers.

panels.title: Rows held vs quarantined (6h increase)
panels.description: Did rows get spilled out of the canonical tree because their archive hour was never corroborated? Held rows are parked pending hour confirmation, and holding is the NORMAL path at every boundary — roughly three rows per boundary is the structural baseline, so this series discriminates nothing on its own. Quarantined rows are the subset actually written to a sidecar file, which the sweep, the merge, the recovery floor and the archive's tree verification all skip; they are kept forever and re-enter the tree only when a live corroborated stream next opens their hour. This is NOT the late-arrival path: a row that genuinely arrives after its hour was finalized is dropped by the late-event guard and counted nowhere. The two real causes are an hour carrying only one live stream, and a capture process stopping within five minutes of an hour boundary. The measured baseline is zero on both capture machines, so any nonzero quarantine value is a real event and pages after `for: 15m`. Both counters are unlabeled totals summed across every pair and kind at the source, so which pair cannot be shown here — no such panel can be built. Runbook: infra/runbooks/capture.md#zcrypto-capture-rows-quarantined. Scoped by the capture-machine picker.

panels.title: Capture counters — cumulative since process start
panels.description: How much damage each capture machine has taken over its whole life. Deliberately all-green with no page lines: scale reads here, recency reads on the delta panels beside it. Every series resets when the capture container is recreated, so a step down to zero is a restart, not a repair. Gap seconds are on the right axis because they are the one series here measured in time rather than counts. Scoped by the capture-machine picker.

panels.title: Spool free % (root filesystem)
panels.description: How much runway the unbackfillable capture spool has before the prune ring must be fixed. The spool lives on the root filesystem. The 10 percent line is the early warning, held for `for: 5m` — it fires long before the daemon's own 1 GiB watermark starts discarding, so reaching it means the prune ring broke or an unexpected consumer appeared. Context here: the page for this line points at the fleet board, which plots the same ratio for every machine. Scoped by the capture-machine picker.

panels.title: Hard stops — disk watermark & venue status
panels.description: The two conditions under which capture is no longer trustworthy at the source. A breached disk watermark is not a warning: the book and trade handlers drop every incoming message instead of writing it, the data is unbackfillable, and the daemon also withholds its dead-man ping, so nothing else on that machine can page. It fires on the first breaching sample above 0.5 — no pending period, and by then the discard has already been running for up to 90 s, because the daemon re-checks the watermark every 30 s and the gauge is scraped every 60 s. The venue counter has a series only for states the daemon has actually seen, so it is EMPTY while the venue is online — the trailing zero fallback keeps the panel at 0 rather than blank, and the `on()` in it is load-bearing: without it the fallback stops being mutually exclusive and rides through as a permanent extra series. Any non-online state pages after `for: 5m`, and the state decides the response: maintenance is planned and you wait, cancel-only or post-only mean the venue is degraded. That counter is born at 1 on the event and latches until the daemon restarts, which is why the alert is presence-based rather than an increase. Scoped by the capture-machine picker.

targets.expr: sum by (host, system) (zcrypto_capture_venue_status_total{host=~"$capture_host", system!="online"}) or on() vector(0)

panels.title: Segments written & bytes (1h increase)
panels.description: Is the writer still committing hourly segments at normal size while the process stays up? Both counters are unlabeled totals summed across every pair and kind at the source, so per-pair write counts do not exist and cannot be charted — the only per-pair evidence available is silence, staleness and desync, on the panels above. No alert watches either series. Scoped by the capture-machine picker.

panels.title: Hour-rotation residuals — early closes, past-dated opens & clock offset
panels.description: Three signals that only mean anything read together, because each of the three faults they cover is invisible to at least one of them. Early closes count archive hours the writer finalized before its own clock said the hour was over: a bogus exchange timestamp closing an hour early and a host clock running a few minutes behind produce the identical series, so this one names no cause on its own and pages only as a warning. Past-dated opens count streams whose FIRST event was stamped into an hour already gone — that publishes an hour marked complete for a period nothing was captured. It can step at most once per stream per capture process, its baseline is a hard zero over the fleet's whole life, and any step pages critical. The absolute clock offset on the right axis is the third, and it is not redundant with the first: a clock running AHEAD closes hours early and subtracts its own lead back out of the early-close measurement, so it is invisible there and this is its only evidence — which is why an offset past 10 seconds, or a machine reporting its clock unsynchronised, pages critical on its own. Read the counters against the offset: early closes with a healthy clock mean a bad timestamp and permanent loss on that stream, early closes with a lagging clock mean the clock and cost nothing. The truncation is never repairable once it has happened; the offset is the only one of the three you can act on before the damage. Runbook: infra/runbooks/capture.md#bogus-timestamp-hour-rotation. The clock series exist on the capture machines only. Scoped by the capture-machine picker.

panels.title: Mirror lag by source & reconciler liveness
panels.description: Are both mirrors still producing, and is the reconciler that compares them still running? Lag is per mirror side, so the alert instance names which side went quiet; either side above 3 hours pages after `for: 10m`. One to two hours of lag is the healthy steady state, because a final only commits after its hour closes and the pull is hourly. If it is the SECONDARY side, the fleet has no witness and the next primary gap is permanent. The liveness series is now minus the reconciler's last clean cycle and pages above the same 3 hours after `for: 5m` — the exported file is scraped in place, so a dead reconciler holds its last value forever and only the timestamp reveals it. Same number, two different alerts. Cycle duration is how long that last clean cycle took, start to publish. It does not add to the liveness age above — the stamp is written at completion, so consecutive publishes stay one tick apart no matter how long a cycle runs. What a long cycle threatens is cadence: the tick is every 30 minutes, so a duration approaching that means the next trigger fires against a still-running unit and is dropped, halving the booking rate — the red line on the duration series at 1,500 s is where that warning fires. The skipped-hours series is a COUNT, not seconds (its own axis unit), and it is the first thing to read beside a slow cycle: a settled window hour whose inputs have not changed is skipped rather than re-examined, so a steady zero means every hour is being re-examined and the duration will keep tracking the window's data volume. Runbook: infra/runbooks/ops.md#zcrypto-reconcile-cycle-duration. Published only by the ops machine. The only per-pair evidence for a lagging mirror is on the capture row above: a per-pair write count does not exist.

panels.title: Gap outcome — last 24h
panels.description: Did loss and healing pressure happen IN THE LAST DAY — the panel that answers "is the red number new?" without leaving the board. Both series carry their alerts' own reset guard, and that is load-bearing: a deliberate ledger correction reads to the time-series store as a counter reset, and a bare increase would report the whole post-reset value as fresh permanent loss — painting this panel red at the exact moment the alert, hardened against precisely this, correctly stays silent. Residual seconds are silence NEITHER mirror covered, so they can be neither healed nor backfilled; any increase above zero pages immediately, with no hold at all (`for: 0s`). The healable series is divided by the live pair count exactly as its alert divides it, and pages above 600 after `for: 30m`. That divisor is plotted beside it and is the FULL pair count, not a count of desynced pairs — the gauge it counts is emitted for every pair on every scrape, so a flat twelve is health. The divisor is deliberately left unscoped, as the alert writes it: scoping it would make this panel disagree with the page whenever the two capture machines' pair sets differ, which is exactly what adding a pair creates for one converge window. Published only by the ops machine.

targets.expr: ((increase(zcrypto_reconcile_healable_gap_seconds_total{host="ops"}[24h]) > 0 and resets(zcrypto_reconcile_healable_gap_seconds_total{host="ops"}[24h]) == 0) or on() vector(0)) / scalar(count(count by (pair) (zcrypto_capture_book_desynced)) or vector(1))

panels.title: Dark-episode verdict split — cumulative since ledger genesis
panels.description: The both_streams_silent seconds from the panel above, split by what the evidence weighs toward: venue_silent (both capture hosts recorded the same venue message timestamps inside the episode -- the silence was upstream of both), capture_divergent (one host missed what the other received), and undetermined (no evidence either way, including every episode recorded before this split existed). A parallel view, not an alternative count -- it never pages: venue silence is not an actionable fault, and the sum of the three never exceeds the residual total beside it. Read during triage of the residual-gap page, to see whether the silence was upstream or a capture-side miss. Published only by the ops machine.

panels.title: Gap totals — cumulative since ledger genesis
panels.description: A number here is history, not an incident. Lifetime scale in each of the three outcomes, all-green with no page lines — recency lives on the panel beside this one, which carries the page lines and the reset guard. The record count is the explanatory series: it is how many append-only ledger records the cycle summed its totals from, so a step DOWN in any counter is legible as a deliberate ledger correction rather than a mystery. That matters precisely because the guarded panel beside this one correctly reads zero after a correction, which also makes the correction invisible there. Published only by the ops machine.

panels.title: Reconcile output — hours minted (24h)
panels.description: Is the healer actually writing hours into the overlay? This is what separates "nothing was broken" from "the healing step is not running". Spliced hours are book hours minted from a primary-plus-secondary splice; union hours are trade hours minted from a cross-machine trade-id union. No alert watches either. Published only by the ops machine.

panels.title: Trade reconciliation — deficit & dedup rows (24h)
panels.description: How many trade rows each mirror was missing that the other had — the only measure of whether the two trade streams are genuinely redundant. **Read the selector before editing it**: the deficit counter is emitted with its OWN host label carrying a mirror SIDE rather than a machine name, and the fleet-wide machine stamp is only applied where that label is absent, so it never lands on this family. Selecting the publishing machine here renders this panel permanently empty. The duplicate-row counter is an ordinary single-publisher series. Published only by the ops machine. No alert watches either.

panels.title: Ledger scan — cost and size
panels.description: How expensive the append-only ledger has become to read. Every cycle loads the WHOLE file and sums it, so both halves are O(ledger); this is their measured wall-clock cost, with the record count beside it as the leading indicator. Measured on synthetic ledgers (`infra/scripts/bench-ledger-scan.py`, re-runnable): the scan is linear at roughly 3 microseconds per record, and memory — not time — binds first, because every record becomes a Python dict held in a list at about six times the file's size on disk. Time degrades gently; memory does not, and a cycle killed by the OOM reaper publishes nothing at all, so the cycle-duration alert beside this one goes STALE rather than high. That is the gap the two alerts on this series exist to cover: warning at 10 s, where the ledger has become the cost driver and is worth re-measuring; critical at 30 s, about a quarter of the memory the host had available when the bar was set, with the wall roughly four times further out. Both are several orders of magnitude above the live ledger, so neither is a near-term expectation.

panels.title: Verify-replay — run verdict
panels.description: Did the sweep complete at all? A crash, an I/O error, or a mount that silently resolved empty all present as a run that did not complete, while every count below stays frozen at its carried-forward value — so today's findings are unknown, not clean. It pages below 1 after `for: 15m`. The exit code sits beside it as context ONLY and is deliberately uncoloured: it stays at 1 forever once any hour has ever failed, which is exactly why alerting on it was retired in favour of the change-based rule on the panel below, and colouring it here would rebuild that red-forever defect next to the panel that replaced it. Published only by the ops machine.

panels.title: Verify-replay — freshness (last run vs last clean run)
panels.description: Is the nightly sweep still firing at all, separately from whether its runs come back clean? **No alert watches either age**, so this panel is the only coverage that exists for a sweep that has simply stopped running — nothing will page. A healthy pattern is a daily sawtooth on both. A last-clean stamp of zero means the sweep has never completed cleanly, in which case the age renders as time since the epoch rather than a small number and will flatten every other series on the axis. Published only by the ops machine.

targets.legendFormat: age of last run (clean or not)

panels.title: Verify-replay — hour ledger
panels.description: Where every canonical hour sits, and whether the total still balances against replayed plus reused plus pending. Context for the breakage panel below — no alert reads these counts directly. All of them are carried forward unchanged when a run breaks before reporting, so read them together with the run verdict, or a frozen ledger looks like a stable one. Published only by the ops machine.

panels.title: Verify-replay — new breakage & backlog drift
panels.description: Did a NEW hour break, or has the backlog stopped draining? A known bad hour is a constant in the failed-hour count and contributes nothing to the 25-hour change, so only an hour that failed today and did not fail in the prior sweep moves that series above zero — and it pages immediately, with no hold at all (`for: 0s`), because a re-failing known hour is exactly what this replaced. The backlog page is a conjunction this panel cannot draw as a single line: it needs pending hours above zero AND the 26-hour change at or above zero, held for `for: 27h`. So a backlog drained to zero shows the change series sitting on its coloured step while the alert correctly stays silent — read the two series together. Note the direction on that series: at or above zero is the fault, and a NEGATIVE change is the healthy drain. Published only by the ops machine.

panels.title: Verify-replay — audit mismatches & sweep duration
panels.description: Does the checkpoint the sweep reuses hours from still agree with a fresh replay — the only signal that a reused hour is verified rather than skipped. The mismatch count is a GAUGE carried forward from the last sweep that reported one, not a counter, so its recent view is a 25-hour change: an increase-style read would show it flat forever. Sweep duration sits beside it on the right axis so a lengthening sweep is visible before it starts colliding with the drain budget. No alert watches either. Published only by the ops machine.

panels.title: Job exit codes
panels.description: Did each of the five canonical-tree writers come back clean on its last pass? Any non-zero value pages on four of them, after `for: 5m` — but they are not equally severe: a failed panel materialize costs freshness on derived, recomputable data, while a verified-path mismatch or a failed trade backfill means the canonical result itself is in question, and those two are the critical pair. On the overlay-writer cycle, a gate skip and a trade-backfill failure both leave the code at zero; only the reconcile step sets it non-zero, and the backfill has its own series here. Published only by the ops machine. The tape-bars materializer is the fifth and is plotted unlined: a day it cannot publish yet is not an error, so its refusals show up as counts on its own panel rather than here, and only an unexpected failure — a corrupt segment, an unwritable output — lifts this series off zero.

panels.title: Job last-success age
panels.description: How long since each writer last completed cleanly, each against the exact budget its own alert uses: 3 hours for the half-hourly overlay-writer cycle, about six missed cycles; 48 hours for the daily verified-path replay and 48 hours for the daily trade backfill, two missed days each. Two distinct budgets across three series, so each series carries its own bar and there is no shared ladder. All three page after `for: 5m`. The panel materialize has no staleness alert at all and is plotted unlined. A stamp of zero means never succeeded, which renders as time since the epoch rather than a small number and will flatten everything else on the axis. Published only by the ops machine. The tape-bars materializer contributes two series, and the second is the one that matters: its not-yet-healed path completes cleanly by design, so a stalled healer leaves the clean-run stamp advancing every hour while the dataset stops growing. Only the since-a-day-was-last-published series can see that, and a healthy pipeline publishes at least one day per pair per day.

targets.legendFormat: tape-bars — since a day was last published (no page line)

panels.title: Did it run at all? — last-run age
panels.description: Separates a timer that stopped firing from a job that fires and fails. The sawtooth is the signal: each series should drop to near zero on every tick of its own cadence. A rising ramp with no reset is the fault — the timer is not firing, which the exit-code and last-success panels cannot distinguish from a job that runs and succeeds. No alert watches any of these, so this panel is the only place that distinction is visible. Published only by the ops machine.

panels.title: Verified-path lag & trade repairs
panels.description: How far the verified path has fallen behind, and whether trade hours are being repaired NOW or merely were at some point. Days behind is zero when the replay is fully caught up. The repair counter is a true monotone counter — the emitter reads its own previous value and adds — so the 24-hour increase beside it is what answers "now", while the cumulative line answers "ever". No alert watches either. Published only by the ops machine.

panels.title: Tape-bars — days published, refused & permanently missing
panels.description: The tape-bars materializer sweeps hourly and publishes a day of 15m bars once that day's trade tape is measured contiguous. Days published sits at zero most of the time: a day becomes eligible about a day after it ends, so one tick a day carries a one and the rest carry nothing — the flat line is the healthy shape, not a stall. Refused counts settled days whose trade sequence still has a hole; they are retried while the heal window still reaches them, and a steady one for a pair that left the capture set is documented noise rather than a fault. Permanently missing is the irreversible one: a settled day that fell past the retry window with no file will never be published, and nothing else in the fleet reports it. Days in error counts unexpected failures — a corrupt segment, an unwritable output — each costing exactly one day rather than the whole sweep. Published only by the ops machine.

targets.legendFormat: days refused — tape not healed yet

panels.title: Gate verdict
panels.description: Does the fleet currently satisfy its own admission gate, and how long has it held? Deliberately informational, with a text mapping and no red: the gate is met only after at least fourteen consecutive clean days, so not-yet-met is the CORRECT and expected state for the entire accumulation window, and a red tile for a fortnight of healthy days is alarm fatigue in visual form. No alert reads this verdict — the signal that something actually broke is the streak going BACKWARDS, which is on the panel beside this one. Published only by the NAS.

panels.title: Streak & mismatch trend
panels.description: Is the streak climbing or was it reset, and is the mismatch behind it recent or ancient? The streak only ever increments on a clean complete day or resets to zero on a failed one, so a NEGATIVE 6-hour change is the failure and nothing else produces one — which is why the page line on that series sits BELOW zero rather than above it. It fires after `for: 5m` and auto-resolves as the window rolls past, one alert per broken run rather than a drumbeat. At least one replay mismatch or validation failure in the last day pages after `for: 5m` as well. The raw streak is context on the right axis and carries no line. Published only by the NAS.

panels.title: Exporter freshness, duration & journal pull lag
panels.description: Is the verdict on screen fresh, is the journal it was computed from current, and is a slow export still running or did it die? Two different bars on one panel, so each series carries its own: no successful export in over 2 hours pages after `for: 5m`, and a newest journaled cycle more than 6 hours old pages after `for: 5m`. Those bars are not interchangeable — the pull-lag floor is the trading cycle's own 4-hourly cadence rather than a measure of pull health, which is why it sits so much higher. Export duration is context with no line; read it beside export age to tell a slow run from a dead one. Published only by the NAS.

panels.title: Scoring cache — is the journal still being re-hashed?
panels.description: A stalled scoring cache is indistinguishable from a healthy one everywhere except these four numbers, because a cache hit skips the only place the journal's parquet bytes are ever re-hashed. The oldest cycle's verification age pages above 3 days after `for: 15m` — a full rotation is about a day, so that is roughly three sweeps of slack. An EMPTY series here is EXPECTED, not a fault: the exporter emits that gauge only when the scoring cache is active and non-empty, and its alert treats no data as OK for exactly that reason. Cycles replayed should be above zero on every run; a cache that stopped rotating shows replayed at zero with hits at the full count. The invalidated flag is a per-run 0 or 1 rather than a counter, so its recent view is a 24-hour MAXIMUM — "did it happen at all today" is the only meaningful read of it. Published only by the NAS.

panels.title: NAS pull · verify seconds per channel
panels.description: Per-channel wall time the pull spent re-hashing pulled segments against their sidecars this cycle. `full` scope re-hashes everything every cycle; `incremental` hashes only rsync's transfers plus a rotating slice, so a channel's line should be flat and low except on its slice cycle. Published only by the NAS.

panels.title: NAS pull · segments hashed vs walked
panels.description: How many segments existed in the destination tree this cycle versus how many were actually re-hashed. Under `incremental` scope the hashed count should sit well below walked; under `full` scope the two track each other. A hashed count stuck at walked after switching to incremental means the scope setting did not take. Published only by the NAS.

panels.title: Log shipping — dropped vs shipped (6h)
panels.description: Was any log line discarded before it reached the log store — the one fault that makes every log-based alert's SILENCE meaningless, because those rules then reason over an incomplete stream. The measured baseline over seven days is zero on every machine, so any drop in 6 hours is real and pages after `for: 15m`. The cumulative total sits beside it, all-green, so old damage is legible without being mistaken for new. Shipped lines on the right axis give the scale to read a drop against. Legends name the machine and the daemon together, because one machine runs two shippers and the machine name alone is ambiguous there. Scoped by the shipping-machine picker.

panels.title: Log shipping — worker liveness
panels.description: Is the shipper alive? Read CYCLE age for that, and only that: the worker cycles every second and advances that gauge even on an idle cycle, stalling only while it is stuck retrying a push it cannot complete or the thread is wedged. It is the series the page reads — above 5 minutes, held for `for: 10m`, which is about three hundred missed cycles. Last-ship age is context and deliberately carries NO line: the worker skips the push on an empty buffer, so on a healthy quiet machine cycle age reads seconds while last-ship age reads tens of minutes at the same instant. Read it only together with the shipped-line count beside it. That series is also absent until the worker has completed one successful ship, which is expected rather than a fault. What neither series catches is a permanently rejected batch: it still completes a cycle and still advances the liveness gauge, and shows up as dropped lines on the panel beside this one. Legends name the machine and the daemon together. Scoped by the shipping-machine picker.

panels.title: Liquidations poller
panels.description: Is the poller still landing cycles, and has any outage exceeded the 30-hour window the next cycle would re-fetch for free? **No alert watches any of these series**, so this panel is their only coverage. Poll cycles are split by outcome, so a poller that keeps running while every fetch fails is visible as a cycle count with no successes. The age of the last successful cycle is the one to read during an outage: a gap shorter than 30 hours self-heals on the next cycle at no cost, a longer one loses data the window will not re-fetch. Published only by the ops machine.

list.name: capture_host
list.label: Capture host
list.query: Capture primary : zcrypto, Capture secondary : zcrypto-red
list.description: Which capture machine the panels below select. All expands to both machines joined into one matcher, and it is the deliberate default: a fault on one and not the other IS the diagnosis. The option list is the pin — a stray label value cannot appear here — and it is a second place to edit if a third capture machine ever joins.

list.name: pair
list.label: Pair
list.description: Chained to the capture-machine picker, so deselecting a machine drops its pairs. At twelve pairs across two machines the All view is legible; narrowing is for chasing one stuck stream.

list.name: logship_host
list.label: Shipping host
list.description: Scopes the two log-shipping panels and nothing else — named for its scope on purpose, because a picker called Host that governs two of thirty panels is a trap. Derived from a shipping family, so its domain is exactly the machines that run a shipping worker; four daemons across three machines publish it, which is why those legends name the daemon as well.
